title: Confucius
summary: This document is a comprehensive encyclopedic article about Confucius (c. 551 – c. 479 BCE), the Chinese philosopher whose teachings formed the foundation of Confucianism. The article begins with an overview of Confucius's life, his core philosophical teachings (including filial piety, the Silver Rule, and moral governance), and the historical trajectory of Confucianism from the Han dynasty's official adoption through Neo-Confucianism and New Confucianism. It explains the origin of his Latinized name and details his life story, including his humble early years in the state of Lu, his political career culminating in his role as Minister of Crime and his attempts to dismantle the fortifications of powerful aristocratic families, his subsequent self-imposed exile traveling among Chinese states, and his final years teaching thousands of disciples. The philosophy section examines his ethics as a form of virtue ethics, discussing key concepts such as lǐ (ritual propriety), yì (righteousness), and rén (benevolence), along with his political thought favoring rule through virtue and rites rather than coercion, and his views on music and poetry. The article also covers Confucius's extensive legacy: the elaboration of his teachings by followers like Mencius and Xunzi, competition with Legalism, the rise of Neo-Confucianism under Zhu Xi, translations by Jesuit missionaries, and influence on Western thinkers. Additional sections document his pioneering role as an educator with roughly 3,000 students, his disciples, visual and fictional portrayals, memorial ceremonies across China, Taiwan, and South Korea, his extraordinary family lineage—including the title of Duke Yansheng, descendants in Korea, famous modern descendants, and DNA genealogy projects—and concludes with criticism of Confucius, particularly during China's Cultural Revolution.
